items.title: Why a same-handle, different-value entry becomes a conflict
items.body:
The key is right: it records a conflict with the reason "Existing entry differs; update policy must be reviewed." `buildPlan` looks for a target entry with the same handle. If it finds one, it compares the two entries with `canonical`. Equal goes to `unchanged`; different goes to `conflicts`. The tool has no update operation, so it will not decide which value should win.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Plans an update that overwrites the target": the planner only creates; update policy is a practice exercise.
- "Marks it unchanged because the handle matches": the handle finds the match, but the content must also be equal.
- "Creates it under a suffixed handle": no code renames handles; that would also break the idea that the handle is the identity.

excerpts.quote: if (canonical(match) !== canonical(entry)) conflicts.push({ type: definition.type, handle: entry.handle, reason: 'Existing entry differs; update policy must be reviewed.', }); else unchanged.push({ type: definition.type, handle: entry.handle });

readMore.why: Exercise 2 asks you to design deliberate update planning.

items.title: Why one reference field blocks the whole definition
items.body:
The key is right: the whole definition becomes a conflict. In `buildPlan`, if any field definition's type contains the word `reference`, the planner pushes a conflict with the reason "Reference fields require cross-store ID mapping; no fields will be silently dropped." and then `continue`s, which skips the definition and all its entries. A product ID belongs to its source store; copied into a different store it points at nothing real.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Copies the product IDs as-is": the concepts guide says copying an ID does not establish a valid relationship.
- "Sets every reference to null": there is no such code, and it would lose data silently.
- "Creates the definition without the reference field": the reason string itself says no fields will be silently dropped.

excerpts.quote: if (definition.input.fieldDefinitions.some((f) => f.type.includes('reference'))) {
'Reference fields require cross-store ID mapping; no fields will be silently dropped.',
Reference values add another boundary: a product ID belongs to its source store. Copying it into another store does not establish a valid relationship.

readMore.why: Exercise 3 asks you to design the cross-store reference mapping.

items.title: Normalize first, then compare: how the planner sees two stores
items.body:
The planner never compares raw exports. It first runs `normalizeSnapshot` on each one. That function checks the shape (format version, API version, store name), checks that names are unique, checks that each entry's fields match the definition, and then puts its collections into a fixed order. Order matters because a reviewer must be able to trust a diff. Read the sorting and hashing helpers to see exactly which parts are reordered.

After that, `buildPlan` walks the source definitions. Then it walks the entries of each definition and places each into one of four lists: `operations`, `conflicts`, `unchanged` and `targetOnly`. For every list, find the exact condition in the code that sends a definition or an entry there, and which operation kinds can appear in `operations` at all.

The key idea from the concepts guide is identity. A definition is identified by its `type`, an entry by its `handle`. Those names are what the planner matches on. When you read the planner, track which branch each case lands in and what reason string it records.

excerpts.quote: A deterministic planner produces the same operations from equivalent snapshots. This implementation normalizes ordering before hashing and comparison.
Definition types and entry handles form business identities; field keys identify values inside an entry.
`normalizeSnapshot` validates identities, fields, values and supported structure, then sorts collections for deterministic comparison.

readMore.why: Walks normalizeSnapshot and buildPlan in prose, branch by branch.

items.title: What a failure at operation 2 leaves behind
items.body:
The key is right: creates 0 and 1 stay, and the receipt says it stopped at index 2. In the `catch` block of `applyPlan`, the result's status becomes `'stopped'`, `failed` records the index and message, the journal is written once more (a journal error here is swallowed so the real failure is kept), and an error is thrown that says "earlier creates may exist. Re-export before retrying." The loop does not continue.

Nothing is undone. The concepts guide says the journal records confirmed creates but cannot roll back remote operations.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Records 2 as failed and continues": the `catch` throws, which ends the loop.
- "0 and 1 are rolled back": there is no rollback code; the journal is a recovery aid only.
- "Retries with backoff": mutation failures stop execution, because a retry could create a duplicate.

excerpts.quote: result.status = 'stopped'; result.failed = { index, message: error.message };
'Apply stopped; earlier creates may exist. Re-export before retrying.',
The journal records confirmed creates, but it cannot roll back earlier remote operations.

items.title: Why planning a store onto itself throws
items.body:
The key is right: `buildPlan` throws "Source and target stores must differ." It is the first check after both snapshots are normalized, before the operations list even exists. So no plan is produced at all. `applyPlan` repeats the same idea on the clients: it refuses if the source client and target client point at the same store.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Logs a warning and continues": there is no logging here; the code throws.
- "Plans creates for every entry, duplicating them": planning never starts.
- "Returns an empty plan marked unchanged": an empty plan would still be a plan; the code throws instead of returning.

excerpts.quote: if (source.store === target.store) throw new Error('Source and target stores must differ.');
sourceClient.store === targetClient.store ) throw new Error('Explicit target confirmation and matching clients are required.');

items.title: What canonical() sorts, and what it leaves alone
items.body:
The key is right: the two objects match, the two arrays do not. `canonical` is `JSON.stringify(stable(value))`. Read `stable`: for an array it only maps each element through `stable`, keeping the order. For an object it rebuilds it from `Object.keys(value).sort()`, so key order stops mattering. `[1, 2]` and `[2, 1]` stay different strings.

That is why `normalizeSnapshot` sorts its lists explicitly (fields by key, entries by handle, definitions by type). Order inside an array can be meaningful, as in the operations list, so `stable` does not guess.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Neither pair matches": object keys are sorted, so the objects do match.
- "Both match, arrays are sorted too": `value.map(stable)` does not sort.
- "Arrays match but objects do not": this is the reverse of what the code does.

excerpts.quote: if (Array.isArray(value)) return value.map(stable);
Object.keys(value) .sort()
.sort((a, b) => a.handle.localeCompare(b.handle));

items.title: Why one conflict stops every create
items.body:
The key is right: nothing is sent. Inside `applyPlan`, after the fresh plan is rebuilt and compared, there is one line that checks `current.conflicts.length`. If it is not zero, it throws "Plan has conflicts; no mutation was sent." This happens before the first journal write and before the loop that calls `createRemote`. So the 3 valid creates never run either. The worked-change guide says this on purpose: a mixed plan should not be partly applied while hiding unresolved differences.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Only the creates before the conflict": conflicts are not in the operations array at all, and the check runs before any operation.
- "The 3 creates; the conflict is skipped": that is exactly the partial apply the guide rules out.
- "Creates plus a placeholder": the planner has no placeholder operation; it only has createDefinition and createEntry.

excerpts.quote: if (current.conflicts.length) throw new Error('Plan has conflicts; no mutation was sent.');
Any remaining conflict also stops all creates, including otherwise valid missing resources.

items.title: Why an empty string fails a required field
items.body:
The key is right: normalization throws "Required entry field is missing." Look at the check inside `normalizeSnapshot`. For every field the definition marks as required, it looks for an entry value with the same key whose value is not `null` and not `''`. An empty title fails the `v.value !== ''` part, so no value matches and the error is thrown. This happens while the snapshot is normalized, before any plan exists.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Having the key is enough": the check tests the value too, not just the key.
- "Skipped and reported in targetOnly": `targetOnly` is for target entries missing from the source, and normalization throws rather than skipping.
- "Passes now, rejected later by the target": the error happens locally, before anything is sent anywhere.

excerpts.quote: field.required && !values.some((v) => v.key === field.key && v.value !== null && v.value !== '') ) throw new Error('Required entry field is missing.');

items.title: Start here: from a copy script to a reviewed migration plan
items.body:
This repo is a small Node tool that copies Shopify "metaobjects" (custom content types called definitions, plus their entries) from one store to another. The course in `astraupskill/` treats it as a study of careful integration work: what can you safely conclude from a snapshot, a response, or a half-finished run?

Suggested reading order:

1. `astraupskill/README.md` for the glossary (snapshot, plan, conflict, journal). Keep that table open.
2. `01-CODEBASE-MAP.md`: the three boundaries, the CLI command, the planner and the HTTP client.
3. `02-CONCEPTS.md`: determinism, hashes, the three layers of success, and why output models are not input models.
4. `03-WORKED-CHANGE.md` with `scripts/lib/planner.js` open beside it.
5. `05-PRACTICE.md` section 0 (warm-ups that run offline), then `07-TRACE-LAB.md`.

Everything in the core course runs on fixture files with plain Node. You do not need a Shopify account. Most quizzes in this pack ask what `buildPlan` or `applyPlan` does in one situation, so read `planner.js` slowly, one `if` at a time.

excerpts.quote: These commands use synthetic fixtures and local test boundaries. You do not need a Shopify account or token to complete the core course.
[planner.js](../scripts/lib/planner.js) is mostly pure data transformation.

readMore.why: The glossary table maps each term to the function where it lives.
A one-page tour of the command, planner and client boundaries.

items.title: Why a target-only entry is listed, never deleted
items.body:
The key is right: the entry goes into `targetOnly` and is left alone. After the main loop, `buildPlan` walks every entry in the target. If the source has no entry with the same type and handle, it pushes it to `targetOnly`. That list is just for review. The planner has no delete operation at all, and the concepts guide explains why: absence from one export is not proof the record should go.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Copies it back into the source snapshot": the planner never changes its inputs; the code map says it never mutates the input fixtures.
- "Records it as a conflict": conflicts are pushed only inside the source loop, for source items. Target-only entries do not block apply.
- "Plans a delete": there is no delete operation; deletion policy is left as a practice exercise.

excerpts.quote: targetOnly.push({ type: definition.type, handle: entry.handle });
target-only entries are reported and retained because absence from a source export is not enough evidence to delete them.

readMore.why: Exercise 6 asks you to design the deletion policy the tool does not have.

items.title: Why a null optional field disappears from the create input
items.body:
The key is right: the field is left out. When `buildPlan` builds the input for a `createEntry`, it takes the entry's fields, keeps only those whose value is not `null`, and maps each to just `{ key, value }`. A null optional field never reaches the input. Note that the field's `type` is dropped too; the worked-change guide says the type is used for validation but not sent.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Converted to an empty string": there is no conversion; the filter removes the field.
- "Sent as an explicit null": the filter `f.value !== null` is there exactly to avoid that.
- "The whole entry is rejected as a conflict": null is allowed for optional fields; normalization accepts a value that is text or null, and only required fields must have a value.

excerpts.quote: fields: entry.fields .filter((f) => f.value !== null) .map((f) => ({ key: f.key, value: f.value })),
if (field.value !== null && typeof field.value !== 'string') throw new Error('Entry field value must be text or null.');

items.title: Three layers of success, and what a stopped run leaves behind
items.body:
Talking to an API can go wrong in more places than "the request failed". The concepts guide names three layers. The HTTP layer can return 200. Inside that, the GraphQL envelope can still carry top-level `errors`. Inside that, the mutation payload can carry `userErrors` or simply lack the ID of the thing you wanted to create. The client only records success when all three layers are clean.

A timeout is worse than an error, because you do not know the outcome. The remote store may have saved the record even though your code never saw the reply. Retrying blindly could create a duplicate. Read how the client treats a failed mutation compared with a failed read, and why the guide says the two must differ.

The journal is the tool's running record of creates it has confirmed. Read carefully what the guide says it can and cannot do. When you study `applyPlan`, look at the loop over operations and the `catch` block: what is written, what is thrown, and what message tells the operator what to do next.

excerpts.quote: An HTTP 200 means the transport received a response. The GraphQL envelope may still contain top-level errors. A mutation payload may also contain `userErrors` or lack a created resource ID.
A timeout after sending a mutation creates uncertainty. The remote service may have committed even though the client did not receive its ID.

readMore.why: Draws the timeline of export, compare, create and journal, and marks where outcomes become unknown.

items.title: Why the definition create must come before the entry create
items.body:
The key is right: the entry's type does not exist in the target until its definition is created, and apply runs the operations in order. In `buildPlan`, a missing definition is pushed as `createDefinition` first, and only then does the loop over that definition's entries push each `createEntry`. In `applyPlan`, the `for` loop walks `current.operations` by index, one at a time, waiting for each create. The worked-change guide says it plainly: a definition must exist before its entry can be created.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Sorted alphabetically by kind": the operations list is never sorted; the order comes from the push order.
- "So receipt indices line up with sourceHash": the hash is of the normalized source snapshot, not of operation order.
- "Apply runs operations in parallel": the loop uses `await` inside a plain `for`, so it is sequential.

excerpts.quote: if (!existing) operations.push({ kind: 'createDefinition', type: definition.type, input: definition.input }); for (const entry of definition.entries) {
for (let index = 0; index < current.operations.length; index++) {
Execution is sequential. A definition must exist before its entry can be created.

items.title: Why a hand-edited plan cannot sneak in an extra create
items.body:
The key is right: apply refuses. `applyPlan` does not trust the plan file. It exports both stores again, calls `buildPlan` on the fresh exports, and compares the canonical text of the whole supplied plan with the whole rebuilt one. An extra createEntry makes the two strings different, so it throws "Plan is stale or changed."

The hashes alone would not catch this, and that is the lesson. The concepts guide says a hash detects changed content; it is not a signature. The hashes describe the snapshots, not the operations, so they still match. That is why apply compares the entire artifact.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Both hashes still match, so it runs": apply does not stop at the hashes; it compares the full plan.
- "Apply skips the hash check when the op count grows": there is no such rule in the code.
- "Only the added create is skipped": the comparison is all-or-nothing; one difference stops the whole apply.

excerpts.quote: const current = buildPlan(source, target); if (canonical(plan) !== canonical(current)) throw new Error('Plan is stale or changed. Export and review a new plan.');
A hash detects changed normalized content; it is not authorization or a digital signature.
